According to multiple sources, teething does not cause true fever in infants [d6][d5]. Mayo Clinic states that teething may cause a "slight increase in temperature — but no fever," and researchers confirm that fever is not an indication of teething [d6]. A prospective PubMed study of 125 children similarly found that while mild temperature elevation was associated with teething, fever over 102°F was not significantly associated with tooth emergence [d5]. A literature review published in the Journal of the American Academy of Pediatrics concluded that tooth eruption can lead to a rise in temperatures, but not to levels characterized as fevers [d4][d3]. If a baby has a true fever (100.4°F or higher), it is more likely a sign of infection or another illness unrelated to teething, and parents should consult a medical provider [d1][d2].
